basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: Taiwan annual rainfall ~2,500mm, ~2.5x world average, but usable water per capita only ~4,074 m3/yr (~1/5 world average) (Water Resources Agency, MOEA). ~80% of rain falls May-Oct; typhoons + summer plum rains supply >50% of annual water; 2021 was the first year since 1964/56 years with no typhoon landfall, triggering the worst drought in decades (WRA; Earth.org; NPR/KPBS Apr 2023). Deji Reservoir sedimentation ~47% of capacity lost (WRA data, widely reported). 2021 drought: 17 of 19 major reservoirs <50%, Baoshan No.2 ~7%, Techi ~4.4%, rationing 2 days/week for >1 million households ~2 months (Earth.org; NPR). National reservoir dredging has exceeded average annual sediment inflow since 2022 (WRA); Shihmen Amuping Desilting Tunnel operating since Sept 2023 (WRA). Hsinchu desalination plant ~13,000 tonnes/day; national pipe leakage fell from ~20% a decade ago to ~14% now (Earth.org). Water price ~NT$11/tonne, several times cheaper than US/UK (Earth.org). Agriculture uses >70% of Taiwan's water but <2% of GDP (Earth.org; multiple sources). Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md.

slides.1: Have you ever noticed Taiwan's strange relationship with water? Some years the government rations our tap water, while other years that same rain floods the very same streets.
slides.2: SDG 6 promises clean water and sanitation for everyone. That means far more than simply having enough water — it means water that stays truly safe, dependable and fairly shared.
slides.3: Taiwan collects around 2,500mm of rainfall annually, roughly 2.5 times the global norm. However, each person here can actually draw on only a fifth of that same figure.
slides.4: Because our mountains are steep and our rivers are short, rainwater rushes into the ocean before engineers can store it. Most of that rain falls between May and October each year.
slides.5: More than half of Taiwan's water each year comes from typhoons and the summer plum rains. That reliable pattern collapsed in 2021. For the first time in 56 years, none made landfall, and severe drought began.
slides.6: There is a quieter danger too, called sediment. Mud washing down from the mountains has silted up our reservoirs, and Deji Reservoir alone has lost about 47% of its storage space.
slides.7: During that 2021 drought, 17 of our 19 major reservoirs dropped below half full, with Baoshan No.2 falling to about 7 percent. Even then, our taps never completely ran dry.
slides.8: Since 2022, crews have officially cleared more mud than flows in each year, say Water Resources Agency figures. A desilting tunnel at Shihmen, running since 2023, clears mud and also lowers flood risk.
slides.9: Supply is slowly diversifying, led by a desalination plant in Hsinchu that now makes about 13,000 tonnes of water daily. Also, pipe leakage has dropped from roughly 20% to about 14%.
slides.10: Taiwan no longer relies on reservoirs alone these days. New pipes can now shift water between river basins during any shortage, and desalination also adds extra supply too.
slides.11: Building new supply is not enough by itself. Taiwan must also keep replacing its aging underground pipes, because water that has already been purified should not simply leak into the ground.
slides.12: Water in Taiwan costs only about NT$11 per tonne, several times cheaper than in the US or the UK. A higher price might encourage saving, but it would burden vulnerable families.
slides.13: Climate change is disrupting the typhoon pattern our reservoirs depend on. Scientists now expect that seasonal timing to become far less predictable in the years ahead of us.
slides.14: However, when typhoons do arrive, the rain now tends to fall in shorter, heavier bursts. Reservoirs cannot fully capture it, so flooding happens instead of steady, useful storage.
slides.15: If a serious drought hits during planting season, farmers can lose their fields to fallowing first. Agriculture takes over 70% of our water supply but earns under 2% of our GDP.
slides.16: This trade-off also reaches many ordinary families too. In 2021, water cuts hit daily life for students and their families for two whole months, so it is not just an idea.
slides.17: To sum up, Taiwan faces heavy rainfall sitting right alongside real water scarcity. A warming climate is making that gap even harder to manage with every passing year.
slides.18: We should reframe this problem, because it is not really about people wasting water carelessly. Geography, old systems and climate are compounding each other, and blame alone misses the real system.
slides.19: So what can students actually do? You can study the public data the Water Resources Agency shares, support pipe and pricing reform, or choose a career in engineering or policy.
slides.20: Taiwan needs fresh thinking for a drier future. Let's stop simply hoping the rain arrives on schedule, and let's start building a system that can handle whatever climate we get.
